overview: Compsognathus longipes was one of the smallest non-avian dinosaurs, about the size of a turkey (0.65–1 m), from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen Limestone of Germany (~150 Ma). For over a century it held the record as the smallest known dinosaur, and the first specimen described was the most complete theropod known at the time — providing crucial evidence that dinosaurs were slender, active animals rather than lumbering reptiles.

The Solnhofen lagoon-margin environment where Compsognathus is found also preserves Archaeopteryx, and the similarity between the two — a small feathered theropod and a small non-feathered theropod of similar size — fuelled early debates about the origin of birds. Its stomach contents in both known specimens include small lizards, confirming it was a fast active predator.

fossilSites.name: Solnhofen Limestone
fossilSites.note: Late Jurassic (Tithonian) lagoonal deposits famous for exceptional preservation; yields Compsognathus alongside Archaeopteryx and a diverse marine fauna.

fossilSites.name: Canjuers Limestone
fossilSites.note: Late Jurassic lagoonal deposits with the larger French Compsognathus specimen.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: The first specimen was found in Bavaria around 1859 and described by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1861, who initially classified it as a lizard. Thomas Henry Huxley recognised its dinosaurian nature and compared it to Archaeopteryx in 1868, arguing that it demonstrated the close relationship between dinosaurs and birds. A second, larger specimen from France described in 1978 may represent a distinct species (C. corallestris or a female with different proportions).

articles.title: Stomach contents and diet
articles.body: Both known specimens preserve the remains of small lizards in the stomach region. The German specimen contains a nearly complete skeleton of Bavarisaurus — a small, fast lizard — implying that Compsognathus was an active pursuit predator capable of catching agile prey. Its two-fingered hand (some relatives have three) shows early reduction of the hand in some coelurosaur lineages.

articles.title: Size and significance
articles.body: Compsognathus was the smallest adult dinosaur known for over a century until the discovery of smaller species in the Cretaceous feathered dinosaur record from China. Its small size, fine bones and active lifestyle made it the archetypal "bird-like" non-avian dinosaur in Victorian science, and it features in Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912) as the miniature dinosaurs encountered by the expedition.

fossilRecord.formations: Solnhofen Limestone, Bavaria, Germany; Canjuers Formation, France
fossilRecord.material: Two articulated skeletons with exceptional soft-tissue detail; one preserves stomach contents.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Jurassic shallow lagoon environments in what are now southern Germany and southern France.
fossilRecord.evidence: Stomach contents document its diet of small lizards; exquisite preservation confirms body outline and limb proportions.

record.description: Compsognathus longipes was a small coelurosaur from the Tithonian lagoonal limestones of Germany and France. Two nearly complete skeletons of different sizes document its slender bipedal body; C. corallestris is generally treated as the same species.
facts: The smaller German specimen contains lizard remains in its abdominal region, direct evidence of predation or scavenging.
The larger French specimen shows that the famously tiny German individual was not the maximum adult size.

presentation.heroLead: A turkey-sized Late Jurassic predator from the Solnhofen lagoons, one of the first small dinosaurs ever found and long a benchmark for the bird-like build of coelurosaurs.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Compsognathus longipes
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of Compsognathus longipes running, shown with a coat of simple filaments
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by Conty based on a modern skeletal reconstruction. The filament covering and colour are modelled on the related Sinosauropteryx; no feathers are preserved on Compsognathus itself.

animalParagraphs: Compsognathus longipes was a lightly built theropod with a small, pointed head, a long neck, slender hindlimbs and a tail that made up about half its length. The German skeleton is under a metre long and was for many years the smallest dinosaur known; the later French specimen is about a third larger.

Its diet is documented unusually well. The German specimen preserves the skeleton of a small lizard, Bavarisaurus, in the region of the gut, showing that it caught or scavenged fast-moving small prey. The forelimbs were short, with hands that Gishlick and Gauthier reinterpreted in 2007 as having two functional fingers and a reduced third.

Compsognathus lived on islands and shorelines of a shallow tropical sea, where fine limestone mud entombed carcasses with remarkable fidelity. The same deposits yield Archaeopteryx, and the two animals were compared closely in nineteenth-century debates about the origin of birds.
animalHighlights: Two articulated skeletons of different sizes are known, one from Germany and one from France.
A lizard skeleton preserved in the gut region of the German specimen is direct evidence of what it ate.
Its slender build and long legs mark it as a fast-moving pursuit predator of small animals.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: A lizard skeleton inside the German specimen shows small vertebrate prey. The wider diet is inferred from the teeth.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long shins and feet relative to the thigh suggest a fast runner; actual speeds are not measured.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Both skeletons are nearly complete, so their lengths are well constrained, but their growth stages and the adult size range are debated.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: No feathers or skin are preserved. A coat of simple filaments is inferred from Sinosauropteryx and other relatives; some authors have suggested scales on the tail.

locality.name: Solnhofen lithographic limestone
locality.note: The holotype came from lithographic limestone quarries near Kelheim in the 1850s; the second specimen was found at Canjuers in southern France in 1971. The map shows the Bavarian type region.

presentation.classificationSummary: Compsognathus is a small coelurosaur and the name-bearer of Compsognathidae, a group that may also include Sinosauropteryx, Juravenator and others. Whether Compsognathidae is a natural group or a grade of small early coelurosaurs is contested.

related.reason: Compare with a closely related Chinese compsognathid that preserves filamentous feathers and colour banding.
Compare with another small theropod from the Solnhofen region, known from a juvenile.
Compare with the early bird found in the same limestones and long contrasted with Compsognathus.

questions.title: Was it feathered?
questions.copy: No feathers are preserved on either specimen. A filament coat is inferred from relatives, and the possibility of scaly patches on the tail has been raised.

questions.title: How old were the two animals?
questions.copy: The German specimen is often called a juvenile and the French one an adult, but bone histology has not settled the growth stage of either.

questions.title: Is Compsognathidae a real group?
questions.copy: Some analyses recover the compsognathids as a clade; others scatter them among early coelurosaurs, sometimes as juveniles of other lineages.

review.ageReviewNote: The Solnhofen and Canjuers lagoonal deposits are Tithonian.

evidence.confidenceLimit: Two good skeletons support anatomy and small-prey feeding; growth stage, feathers and population size range remain uncertain.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Bayerische Staatssammlung für Paläontologie und Geologie, Munich
specimens.note: Articulated skeleton about 89 centimetres long on a Solnhofen limestone slab, with the lizard Bavarisaurus in the gut region.

specimens.name: French referred specimen
specimens.note: Larger articulated skeleton from Canjuers, Var, originally named C. corallestris; referred to C. longipes by Peyer (2006).

panel.headline: Two near-complete articulated skeletons from lagoon limestones.
panel.standfirst: Compsognathus longipes is known from the German holotype, an articulated skeleton on a limestone slab with a lizard in its gut region, and a larger, slightly less complete skeleton from Canjuers in France originally named C. corallestris.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Almost every skeletal region is preserved in articulation in the German specimen and repeated in the French one, but only two individuals exist and parts of the hands, feet and skull are crushed or incomplete.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The skull, complete vertebral column, ribs, gastralia, shoulder and pelvic girdles, forelimbs and hindlimbs of the holotype, all lying articulated on a single slab, plus a comparable but larger skeleton from France.
knownRemains.note: Both skeletons are flattened, and the small hand bones are hard to interpret; the French specimen lacks the skull tip and parts of the limbs. No feathers or skin are preserved.

media.title: Cast of the Compsognathus longipes holotype slab
media.alt: Cast of the Compsognathus longipes holotype skeleton curled on a limestone slab
media.caption: A cast of the German holotype as displayed in Karlsruhe. The skeleton lies in a curled posture typical of Solnhofen fossils; the original slab is held in Munich.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Complete but crushed skull and lower jaws with small, pointed teeth in both specimens.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae with ribs and gastralia; the long tail is nearly complete in the holotype.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Shoulder and pelvic girdles, short forelimbs with disputed finger counts, and long hindlimbs with complete feet in the holotype.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: A lizard skeleton in the gut region of the holotype and possible eggs near the French specimen; no feathers, skin or colour are preserved.

specimenCards.title: BSP AS I 563 · holotype
specimenCards.description: An articulated skeleton about 89 centimetres long on a Solnhofen limestone slab, collected in the 1850s and described by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1859. The gut region contains the lizard Bavarisaurus.
specimenCards.meta: Near Kelheim · Solnhofen Limestone · Bayerische Staatssammlung für Paläontologie und Geologie, Munich

specimenCards.title: MNHN CNJ 79 · French skeleton
specimenCards.description: A larger articulated skeleton found at Canjuers in 1971 and named Compsognathus corallestris by Bidar and colleagues in 1972. Peyer's 2006 restudy referred it to C. longipes and showed the supposed flipper-like hands were an artefact.
specimenCards.meta: Canjuers, Var · Tithonian lithographic limestone · Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Two articulated skeletons, small pointed teeth, long hindlimbs and a lizard preserved in the gut region of the holotype.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A fast, agile predator of small vertebrates; a body covering of simple filaments inferred from feathered compsognathid relatives.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The growth stage of each specimen, the adult size range, the exact number of functional fingers, and whether the animal bore feathers, scales or both.
